steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on scalable neural network kernels (SNNKs), which reinterpret a feedforward layer as a dot product between random-feature embeddings of the input and of the parameters. Cover kernel methods and random features, the connection to neural networks, the benefits, our URF mechanism, and a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Kernel methods and their computational cost
2. Random features as a fix
3. Neural networks and the feedforward layer
4. Our view: FFL as a two-tower dot-product; advantages
5. Universal random features (URFs)
6. Contributions
7. Relation to compression methods

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Kernel methods
- kernel \mathrm{K}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}: two feature vectors (latent embeddings) -> similarity
- among most theoretically principled approaches to statistical ML; effective in many real problems (cite)
- drawback: high complexity, at least quadratic in training set size N; kernel regression \mathcal{O}(N^{3})

2. Random features
- prior work (cite): random feature (RF) map \Phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}, \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Phi(\mathbf{y})] (approximately linearizing the kernel)
- linear kernel approx \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\approx\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{y}}, \widehat{\mathbf{z}}=\Phi(\mathbf{z}); cost dominated by m; gains if m\ll N
- RFs for Gaussian, Matern (cite), polynomial (cite)

3. NNs
- better optimization algorithms + accelerator hardware -> NN models predominant (cite)
- FFL = core module (equation); \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times d},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{l}, activation f element-wise
- expressiveness from stacking FFLs with learnable \mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}; far beyond standard kernel methods

4. Our view
- deep connection between scalable kernels and NNs
- FFL outputs expected vector of dot-products of latent embeddings of input and of parameters; disentangle input from parameters until final dot-product kernel
- \Phi_{f}, \Psi_{f}: f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b)=\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{f}(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w},b)]; \mathbf{w}^{0},...\mathbf{w}^{l-1} transposed rows of \mathbf{W}; expectations dropped in instantiation
- advantages: network compression (O(lm) vs O(ld)); computational savings (sub-quadratic, o(dl)); NN bundling (Sec. 3.3); deep NNs as scalable kernels (full bundling, explicit optimal parameters e.g. mean squared loss, bypass backpropagation)

5. URFs
- new bounded RF mechanism, universal random features; unbiased estimate of f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b) if f has well-defined Fourier Transform (FT), Riemannian or distributional sense
- Fourier analysis + softmax-kernel estimation methods (cite)
- no extra assumptions on f (not even differentiable); \mathrm{K}_{f} need not be PSD -> important since activations usually not PSD kernels

6. Contributions
- SNNK module replacing FFL (Sec. 3, Eq. 2, Fig. 1)
- URFs to build \Phi_{f}, \Psi_{f} and implement SNNKs (Sec. 3.1); trigonometric maps -> SNNK replacements of SIREN networks (cite)
- \mathrm{ReLU} - \mathrm{SNNK} layers (Sec. 3.2), effective downstream (Sec. 4.3.2); related to arc-cosine kernels (cite); SNNKs strictly more expressive than FFLs
- neural network bundling (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 1)
- exhaustive evaluation: point-wise kernel estimation to adapter-based Transformer fine-tuning; about 5x fewer trainable parameters (Sec. 4)

7. Compression
- common: pruning (cite), distillation (cite), quantization (cite)
- SNNK compression novel, orthogonal, combinable

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Consider a kernel function: \mathrm{K}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, which takes two feature vectors that encode latent embeddings of their objects and returns their similarity. Kernel methods are some of the most theoretically principled approaches to statistical machine learning (ML) and they have been effective in many real-world problems. They have theoretical guarantees and can be applied in a rich spectrum of ML settings, but their main drawback is high computational complexity, which is at least quadratic in the size N of the training dataset. For example kernel regression has time complexity \mathcal{O}(N^{3}).

To deal with this, earlier work proposed constructing a random feature (RF) map \Phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} that maps an input point \mathbf{z} to a finite-dimensional feature vector \Phi(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} so that: \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Phi(\mathbf{y})] (so the kernel function is approximately linearized). When general kernels \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) are approximated by linear (dot-product) kernels \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\approx\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{y}} for \widehat{\mathbf{z}}=\Phi(\mathbf{z}) the computational complexity changes a lot, and is now dominated by the number m of random features, so there are computational gains if m\ll N. After that work, many works proposed random features for a broad range of kernels like Gaussian, Matern and polynomial.

Meanwhile, with advances in optimization algorithms for deep ML architectures and in accelerators' hardware, neural network (NN) models have become predominant in machine learning.

The core computational module of NNs is the feedforward layer (FFL), which has the following form:

for \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times d},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{l} (bias) and an activation function f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} (applied element-wise). Deep NNs are much more expressive than standard kernel methods, and this comes from stacking several FFLs together, where each one encodes a non-linear mapping with learnable \mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}.

In this work we make a deep connection between scalable kernel methods and neural networks. We reinterpret the FFL as outputting the expected vector of dot-products of: (1) the latent embeddings of the input \mathbf{x} and (2) the parameters: \mathbf{W},\mathbf{b} of the FFL. This disentangles the input from the model's parameters in the computational graph, and they are only connected in the final computation through the dot-product kernel. More specifically, we think of the FFL as this transformation:

where the mappings: \Phi_{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}, \Psi_{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} satisfy: f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b)=\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{f}(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w},b)] and \mathbf{w}^{0},...\mathbf{w}^{l-1} are the transposed rows of \mathbf{W}. When the layer is instantiated the expectations are dropped. Writing an FFL with two towers, one for the input and one for its learnable parameters, has several advantages:

- network compression: learn \Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w}^{i},b_{i}) for i=0,...,l-1 directly; O(lm) instead of O(ld) parameters; fewer for m\ll d
- computational savings: RFs in o(dl) per point, m\ll d -> FFL time o(dl), sub-quadratic in layer dimensionalities
- deep NN bundling: iterate two-tower representation over multiple FFLs (Sec. 3.3); computational gains
- deep NNs as scalable kernels: bundle all layers -> two-tower factorization of whole NN (Sec. 3.3); explicit optimal parameters for some losses (e.g. mean squared loss); maybe bypass backpropagation

URFs
- new bounded RF mechanism, universal random features (URFs); unbiased estimate of f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b) if f has well-defined Fourier Transform (FT), classical Riemannian or distributional
- Fourier analysis + recent softmax-kernel estimation methods
- note: no extra assumptions on f, not even differentiable; \mathrm{K}_{f} need not be positive semi-definite; important for activations

Contributions
- SNNK module replacing FFL (Sec. 3, Eq. 2, Fig. 1)
- URFs to build \Phi_{f}, \Psi_{f} and implement SNNKs (Sec. 3.1); trigonometric maps -> SNNK versions of SIREN networks
- \mathrm{ReLU} - \mathrm{SNNK} (Sec. 3.2, Sec. 4.3.2); arc-cosine kernels; strictly more expressive than FFLs
- neural network bundling (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 1)
- evaluation from point-wise kernel estimation to adapter-based Transformer fine-tuning; about 5x fewer trainable parameters (Sec. 4)

Compression
- pruning, distillation, quantization; SNNK compression novel, orthogonal, combinable

steps.text:

They have theoretical guarantees and can be applied in a rich spectrum of ML settings, but their main drawback is high computational complexity, which is at least quadratic in the size N of the training dataset. For example kernel regression has time complexity \mathcal{O}(N^{3}).

To deal with this, earlier work proposed constructing a random feature (RF) map \Phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} that maps an input point \mathbf{z} to a finite-dimensional feature vector \Phi(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} so that: \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Phi(\mathbf{y})] (so the kernel function is approximately linearized). When general kernels \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) are approximated by linear (dot-product) kernels \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\approx\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{y}} for \widehat{\mathbf{z}}=\Phi(\mathbf{z}) the computational complexity changes a lot, and is now dominated by the number m of random features, so there are computational gains if m\ll N. After that work, many works proposed random features for a broad range of kernels like Gaussian, Matern and polynomial.

Meanwhile, with advances in optimization algorithms for deep ML architectures and in accelerators' hardware, neural network (NN) models have become predominant in machine learning.

The core computational module of NNs is the feedforward layer (FFL), which has the following form:

for \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times d},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{l} (bias) and an activation function f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} (applied element-wise). Deep NNs are much more expressive than standard kernel methods, and this comes from stacking several FFLs together, where each one encodes a non-linear mapping with learnable \mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}.

In this work we make a deep connection between scalable kernel methods and neural networks. We reinterpret the FFL as outputting the expected vector of dot-products of: (1) the latent embeddings of the input \mathbf{x} and (2) the parameters: \mathbf{W},\mathbf{b} of the FFL. This disentangles the input from the model's parameters in the computational graph, and they are only connected in the final computation through the dot-product kernel. More specifically, we think of the FFL as this transformation:

where the mappings: \Phi_{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}, \Psi_{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} satisfy: f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b)=\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{f}(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w},b)] and \mathbf{w}^{0},...\mathbf{w}^{l-1} are the transposed rows of \mathbf{W}. When the layer is instantiated the expectations are dropped. Writing an FFL with two towers, one for the input and one for its learnable parameters, has several advantages:

- 1. network compression: here, instead of transforming the layer parameters with \Psi_{f}, we can learn the vectors \Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w}^{i},b_{i}) for i=0,...,l-1 directly. Then there are O(lm) trainable parameters instead of O(ld), and for m\ll d the layer has fewer parameters.

- 2. computational savings: if RFs can be constructed in time o(dl) per point and m\ll d, then the overall time complexity o(dl) of the FFL (given pre-computed embeddings \Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w}^{i},b_{i})) is sub-quadratic in the layers' dimensionalities,

- 3. deep NN bundling process: the two-tower representation can be used iteratively to compactify multiple FFLs of NNs, which we call neural network bundling (Sec. 3.3); this also gives computational gains.

- 4. deep NNs as scalable kernels: the extreme version of bundling, with all the layers, gives a two-tower factorization of the whole deep NN, which has several potential practical and theoretical implications (Sec. 3.3). In particular, it gives an explicit formula for the optimal parameters of the fully-bundled network for several loss objectives (e.g. mean squared loss), so it may be possible to bypass backpropagation.

To find the mappings: \Phi_{f}, \Psi_{f} from Eq. 2, we develop a new bounded random feature map mechanism called universal random features (or URFs). URFs give an unbiased estimation of f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b) as long as f has a well-defined Fourier Transform (FT), either in the classical Riemannian or in the distributional sense. To derive URFs we combine Fourier analysis techniques with recent softmax-kernel estimation methods from prior work.

Note: We do not make any additional assumptions on f, and in particular f does not have to be differentiable. Also the function \mathrm{K}_{f} does not need to be positive semi-definite. This is critical for neural networks, where the activation function f usually does not correspond to a positive semi-definite kernel.

Our main contributions in this paper are:

- • We introduce the scalable neural network kernel module (SNNK) to replace a traditional FFL (Sec. 3). It disentangles the network's input and its parameter-set before the final dot-product computation, as in Eq. 2 (see also: Fig. 1).

- • We use our universal random features mechanism (URFs) with SNNKs to efficiently: (1) construct the mappings \Phi_{f} and \Psi_{f} from Eq. 2 and so: (2) implement SNNKs (Sec. 3.1). We give explicit formulae for URFs for trigonometric maps. These give SNNK-based replacements of the SIREN networks from prior work.

- • We propose new NN-layers for a specific SNNK instantiation, called \mathrm{ReLU} - \mathrm{SNNK} (Sec. 3.2), which we found particularly effective in downstream applications (see: Sec. 4.3.2). We show they are related to the class of arc-cosine kernels. Using them we also show that SNNKs are strictly more expressive than regular FFLs, because they can compute functions of the inputs and parameters that cannot be defined as point-wise transformed vectors of their dot-products.

- • We introduce a neural network compactification process using SNNKs, which we call neural network bundling (see: Sec. 3.3 and Fig. 1).

- • We give an exhaustive empirical evaluation of SNNKs, from point-wise kernel estimation to adapter-based Transformers' fine-tuning, with about 5x reduction of the number of trainable parameters (Sec. 4).

Common methods for compressing neural networks are pruning, distillation and quantization. Compressing neural networks with SNNKs is novel and completely orthogonal to these methods, and it can be combined with them.

steps.text:
Consider a kernel function: \mathrm{K}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, taking as input two feature vectors encoding latent embeddings of their corresponding objects and returning their similarity. Kernel methods are among the most theoretically principled approaches to statistical machine learning (ML) and have proven effective in numerous real-world problems [1,2]. Despite their theoretical guarantees and applicability in a rich spectrum of ML settings, the main drawback of these techniques is a high computational complexity, at least quadratic in the size N of the training dataset. For example, kernel regression has time complexity \mathcal{O}(N^{3}).

To address this issue, [3] proposed to construct a random feature (RF) map \Phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} that transforms an input point \mathbf{z} to a finite-dimensional feature vector \Phi(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} such that: \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Phi(\mathbf{y})] (effectively approximately linearizing the kernel function). Approximating general kernels \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) via linear (dot-product) kernels \mathrm{K}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\approx\widehat{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{y}} for \widehat{\mathbf{z}}=\Phi(\mathbf{z}) drastically changes the computational complexity, which is now dominated by the number m of random features, thus providing computational gains if m\ll N. Since that seminal work, a variety of works have proposed random features for a broad range of kernels like Gaussian, Matern [4] and polynomial [5,6,7].

In the meantime, with the advances in the optimization algorithms for deep ML architectures and in the accelerators' hardware, neural network (NN) models [8,9,10] have become predominant in machine learning.

The feedforward layer (FFL) is the core computational module of NNs and has the following form:

for \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times d},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{l} (bias) and an activation function f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} (applied element-wise). The expressiveness of deep NNs, far surpassing standard kernel methods, comes from stacking together several FFLs, each encoding a non-linear mapping with learnable \mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}.

In this work, we draw a deep connection between scalable kernel methods and neural networks. We reinterpret the FFL as outputting the expected vector of dot-products of: (1) the latent embeddings of the input \mathbf{x} and (2) the parameters: \mathbf{W},\mathbf{b} of the FFL, effectively disentangling the input from the model's parameters in the computational graph and connecting them only in the final computation via the dot-product kernel. More specifically, we think about the FFL as the following transformation:

where mappings: \Phi_{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}, \Psi_{f}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m} satisfy: f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b)=\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{f}(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w},b)] and \mathbf{w}^{0},...\mathbf{w}^{l-1} are the transposed rows of \mathbf{W}. In the instantiation of the layer the expectations are then dropped. Rewriting an FFL in terms of two towers, one corresponding to the input and one to its learnable parameters, has several advantages:

- 1. network compression: in the above formulation, instead of transforming layer parameters with \Psi_{f}, one can directly learn vectors \Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w}^{i},b_{i}) for i=0,...,l-1. The number of trainable parameters then becomes O(lm) rather than O(ld), and for m\ll d the layer has a reduced number of parameters.

- 2. computational savings: if RFs can be constructed in time o(dl) per point and m\ll d, the overall time complexity o(dl) of the FFL (given pre-computed embeddings \Psi_{f}(\mathbf{w}^{i},b_{i})) is sub-quadratic in layers' dimensionalities,

- 3. deep NN bundling process: a two-tower representation can be used iteratively to compactify multiple FFLs of NNs, a process we refer to as neural network bundling (Sec. 3.3); this also leads to computational gains.

- 4. deep NNs as scalable kernels: the extreme version of the bundling procedure, involving all the layers, provides a two-tower factorization of the entire deep NN with several potential practical and theoretical implications (Sec. 3.3). In particular, it leads to an explicit formula for the optimal parameters of the fully-bundled network under several loss objectives (e.g. mean squared loss), opening a possibility to bypass backpropagation.

In order to find the mappings: \Phi_{f}, \Psi_{f} from Eq. 2, we develop a new bounded random feature map mechanism, called universal random features (or URFs), that leads to unbiased estimation of f(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}+b) as long as f has a well-defined Fourier Transform (FT), either in the classical Riemannian or distributional sense. To derive URFs, we combine Fourier analysis techniques with recent methods for softmax-kernel estimation from [11].

Note: We do not put any additional assumptions on f; in particular, f is not required to be differentiable. Furthermore, the function \mathrm{K}_{f} does not need to be positive semi-definite. This is critical for applications in neural networks, where the activation function f usually does not correspond to a positive semi-definite kernel.

To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

- • We introduce the scalable neural network kernel module (SNNK) as a replacement of a traditional FFL (Sec. 3), disentangling the network's input and its parameter-set before the final dot-product computation, as given in Eq. 2 (see also: Fig. 1).

- • We accompany SNNKs with our universal random features mechanism (URFs) to efficiently: (1) construct mappings \Phi_{f} and \Psi_{f} from Eq. 2 and consequently: (2) implement SNNKs (Sec. 3.1). We provide explicit formulae for URFs for trigonometric maps, which produce SNNK-based replacements of the SIREN networks from [12].

- • We propose new NN-layers corresponding to a specific SNNK instantiation, called \mathrm{ReLU} - \mathrm{SNNK} (Sec. 3.2), that we found particularly effective in downstream applications (see: Sec. 4.3.2). We show that they are related to the class of arc-cosine kernels [13]. Using them, we also demonstrate that SNNKs are strictly more expressive than regular FFLs, since they allow computing functions of the inputs and parameters that cannot be defined as point-wise transformed vectors of their dot-products.

- • We introduce a neural network compactification process leveraging SNNKs, which we refer to as neural network bundling (see: Sec. 3.3 and Fig. 1).

- • We provide an exhaustive empirical evaluation of SNNKs, from point-wise kernel estimation to adapter-based Transformers' fine-tuning, providing about 5x reduction of the number of trainable parameters (Sec. 4).

Commonly used methods for compressing neural networks are pruning [14], distillation [15] and quantization [16]. Compressing neural networks via SNNKs is novel, completely orthogonal to these methods, and can be combined with them.
